w: A car factory that swallowed a city block, then reinvented itself. Fiat built its cars here on Via Nizza for decades before the plant closed; Renzo Piano folded a multipurpose centre into the old shell, and Fiat's administrative headquarters moved back in. Concrete history wearing a new coat.
s: Fiat's old car factory, reborn by Renzo Piano
_facts: Building complex on Via Nizza that once housed a Fiat car factory
Now houses Fiat's administrative headquarters
Also contains a multipurpose centre designed by architect Renzo Piano

w: Savoy power made stone: a 16th-century palace remodelled by Christine Marie of France with Baroque flourishes from Filippo Juvarra. Its Chapel of the Holy Shroud once housed the Shroud of Turin itself. Nationalised in 1946 and turned into a museum, it joined the Savoy residences' UNESCO listing in 1997.
s: Savoy palace with the Shroud of Turin's chapel inside
_facts: 16th-century House of Savoy palace, modernised in the 17th century by Christine Marie of France with Filippo Juvarra
Includes the Chapel of the Holy Shroud, built to house the Shroud of Turin
Became state property and a museum in 1946
Listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1997 with 13 other Savoy residences

w: The arena where getaway Minis drove over the roof. In 1969's The Italian Job, three Minis are seen driving onto and over Palavela's distinctive curved shell on the bank of the Po — one of the film's most famous scenes. The rest of the time it seats up to 12,200 for less cinematic events.
s: The arena the Minis drove over in The Italian Job
_facts: Indoor arena on the bank of the Po, 130 metres in diameter
Featured in the 1969 film The Italian Job — three Minis drive onto and over its roof
Seats up to 12,200, or 9,200 configured for basketball

n: Basilica of Our Lady Help of Christians
w: Built as part of Don Bosco's safehouse for Turin's poor boys, this Marian shrine now holds his own remains. Pope Pius X raised it to the status of Minor Basilica in 1911. A monument to one man's care for the city's forgotten children, still drawing pilgrims to Santa Maria Ausiliatrice.
s: Don Bosco's shrine, built for Turin's poor boys
_facts: Marian shrine originally part of Don Bosco's safehouse for poor boys
Now contains the remains of Don Bosco
Raised to Minor Basilica status by Pope Pius X in 1911

w: A royal art hoard that has moved house four times. Assembled from Eugene of Savoy's collection and works bought in Genoa, it opened with 365 paintings under King Charles Albert in 1832, then shuttled between palaces for nearly two centuries before reaching the Royal Palace's new wing in 2014.
s: Savoy royal art collection, four house-moves later
_facts: Royal art collection amassed by the House of Savoy over centuries
Inaugurated by King Charles Albert in 1832 with 365 paintings at Palazzo Madama
Moved between several Turin buildings before reaching the Royal Palace's new wing in 2014

w: Turin's Roman skeleton, still standing at full height. The Palatine Gate guarded the north wall of Roman-era Julia Augusta Taurinorum, one of the best-preserved 1st-century Roman gateways anywhere. Since 2006 it anchors an Archaeological Park by the city's old Roman theatre — two thousand years hiding in plain sight.
s: Turin's Roman gate, still standing after 2,000 years
_facts: Roman-era city gate of Julia Augusta Taurinorum (Roman Turin)
One of the world's best-preserved 1st-century AD Roman gateways
Part of an Archaeological Park, opened 2006, alongside the ancient theatre remains

w: A country retreat the city grew up around. Built by the House of Savoy in the 17th century on the hills of Borgo Po, the Villa della Regina was once genuinely rural; Turin has since folded around it. It joined the Savoy residences' UNESCO listing in 1997, its hillside gardens still intact.
s: Savoy hillside retreat the city grew around
_facts: Once semi-rural Savoy palace, now surrounded by the city, in the Borgo Po quarter
Originally built by the House of Savoy in the 17th century
Listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1997 with 13 other Savoy residences

w: Guarino Guarini's Baroque puzzle box, next door to the Royal Palace. Built between 1668 and 1687 as the Royal Church of Saint Lawrence, San Lorenzo is one of the architect-mathematician's great set pieces — geometry doing the work most churches leave to statues.
s: Guarini's Baroque geometry puzzle by the Royal Palace
_facts: Baroque church adjacent to the Royal Palace of Turin, also known as the Royal Church of Saint Lawrence
Designed and built by Guarino Guarini between 1668 and 1687

w: Pier Luigi Nervi's concrete manifesto. Finished in 1948, Torino Esposizioni was built almost entirely from ferrocemento — the thin, wire-reinforced concrete technique Nervi pioneered — proving glass and cement could be as light as they were strong. An engineering trick disguised as an exhibition hall.
_facts: Exhibition hall and convention centre, primarily completed in 1948
Designed by engineer Pier Luigi Nervi
Built with ferrocemento, a thin wire-reinforced concrete technique Nervi pioneered
